content.text: A cryptographic hash function takes any input and produces a fixed-size output. It must be: deterministic, one-way (preimage resistant), and collision resistant.

content.definition: It should be computationally infeasible to find two different inputs that produce the same hash.

content.code:
import hashlib

# SHA-256
hash1 = hashlib.sha256(b"hello").hexdigest()
print(hash1)  # 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824

# SHA-3 (more modern)
hash2 = hashlib.sha3_256(b"hello").hexdigest()

# NEVER use MD5 or SHA-1 for security
# hashlib.md5(b"hello")  # broken, do not use for security

# HMAC for keyed hashing (message authentication)
import hmac
mac = hmac.new(key=b"secret", msg=b"message", digestmod="sha256")
print(mac.hexdigest())

content.text: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes. Use SHA-256 or SHA-3-256 at minimum.

questions.question: What is a preimage attack?
options: Finding two inputs with the same hash
Finding the input from a known hash
questions.explanation: A preimage attack tries to find an input M such that hash(M) equals a known hash value.

faq.q: Can I use SHA-256 to store passwords?
faq.a: No. SHA-256 is too fast — an attacker can try billions of guesses per second. Use bcrypt, Argon2, or scrypt, which are intentionally slow.

examples: Verifying a downloaded file has not been tampered with using SHA-256
